title: Introduction to CSS
subtitle: From Plain HTML to a Real User Interface
description: Learn what CSS is, why it is important, how CSS rules are structured, how selectors work, how CSS connects to HTML, and how to use styling to create a clean application interface.

blocks.text: What Is CSS?
Welcome to CSS.
You are about to learn the language that controls the visual appearance of your web pages.
Before we write any CSS, I want you to understand exactly why CSS exists.
Think about a real application that you use every day.
It probably has colors, spacing, buttons, cards, headings, icons, borders and carefully arranged sections.
HTML by itself can create many of those elements, but it does not provide the complete visual design.
CSS solves that problem.
CSS stands for Cascading Style Sheets.
CSS is a stylesheet language used to describe how HTML elements should be presented.
That presentation includes things such as colors, dimensions, spacing, fonts, borders, backgrounds and positioning.
Here is an important idea to remember.
HTML mainly describes the structure and meaning of the content.
CSS mainly controls the visual presentation of that content.
JavaScript will later allow us to add behavior and interaction.
So you can think of HTML, CSS and JavaScript as three different parts of modern web development.

blocks.question: Which statement describes CSS most accurately?
options: CSS defines the structure and meaning of HTML documents.
CSS controls the visual presentation of HTML elements.
CSS replaces HTML when building a webpage.
CSS is mainly responsible for storing application data.
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. CSS controls the visual presentation of HTML content.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Think about the difference between structure and visual presentation.
blocks.reasoning: HTML provides the structure, while CSS controls how that structure is visually presented.

Open your code editor and create a file called index.html.
Start with this simple page.

blocks.text: Run the page and look at the heading.
Now pause before continuing.
What if we wanted that heading to become blue?

blocks.title: Your First CSS Rule
blocks.output: The h1 heading becomes blue.

blocks.text: Run the page again.
Look at the heading.
The heading should now be blue.
That small piece of code is a CSS rule.
The h1 part is called the selector.
The color part is called the property.
The blue part is called the value.
The selector tells the browser what you want to target.
The property tells the browser what aspect of that target you want to change.
The value tells the browser what setting you want to use.

blocks.title: Understanding the Parts
blocks.output:
The selector is h1.
The properties are color and font-size.
The values are blue and 40px.

blocks.text: Notice that one selector can contain several declarations.
Each declaration normally follows the property-colon-value pattern.
The semicolon separates one declaration from the next.
The braces define the area containing the declarations for that selector.

blocks.question: In the rule h1 { color: blue; }, what is blue?
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. Blue is the value assigned to the color property.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Look at what the browser is being told to use for the color.
blocks.reasoning: In this rule, h1 is the selector, color is the property and blue is the value.

blocks.text: Selectors: Choosing What to Style
A CSS rule is only useful if the browser knows which elements should receive the style.
That is the job of selectors.
The simplest selector is an element selector.
An element selector uses an HTML element name.

blocks.title: Element Selector
blocks.output: Paragraph text becomes gray.

blocks.text: This rule targets paragraph elements.
Now imagine that your page contains five paragraphs.
This selector can apply the same style to all of them.
But what if you only want one particular element to receive a special design?
That is where classes become important.

blocks.title: Adding a Class
blocks.output: Two buttons now have different class names.

blocks.text: The class attribute allows us to give an element a reusable styling label.
In CSS, a class selector begins with a dot.

blocks.title: Class Selectors
blocks.output: The two buttons receive different visual styles.

blocks.text: The primary-button class selects the first button.
The secondary-button class selects the second button.
The important advantage is that a class can be reused.
If several buttons share the same class, one CSS rule can style all of them.
This becomes extremely useful when applications contain many repeated components.

blocks.question: Which CSS selector targets elements with class="card"?
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. A dot is used before a class name.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Remember the symbol used by CSS to identify a class selector.
blocks.reasoning: .card selects elements whose class attribute contains the class name card.

blocks.text: IDs and Specific Elements
There is another selector you should understand before we continue.
It is the ID selector.
An ID identifies a particular element.

blocks.title: Adding an ID
blocks.output: The heading now has the ID main-title.

blocks.text: To select that ID in CSS, use the hash symbol.

blocks.title: ID Selector
blocks.output: The element with ID main-title becomes dark and larger.

blocks.text: A useful rule of thumb is that classes are designed for reusable styling, while an ID represents a particular unique element.
You should not choose an ID simply because it feels more powerful.
Choose a selector based on what you are actually trying to target.
For reusable interface components, classes are usually the better choice.

blocks.question: Which selector correctly targets id="main-title"?
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. IDs are selected with the # symbol.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Look at the difference between a class selector and an ID selector.
blocks.reasoning: The # symbol tells CSS that main-title is an ID selector.

blocks.text: Colors, Backgrounds and Text
Now let's move from selecting elements to actually designing them.
One of the most common CSS tasks is controlling color.
The color property changes the foreground color of text.

blocks.title: Text Color
blocks.output: The heading becomes blue.

blocks.text: The background property controls the background of an element.

blocks.title: Background Color
blocks.output: The application card receives a white background.

blocks.text: CSS also supports different ways of describing colors.
You can use named colors, hexadecimal values, RGB values and other supported color formats.
Hexadecimal colors are especially common in modern interface design.

blocks.title: Common Color Formats
blocks.output: All three declarations describe a blue color using different formats.

blocks.text: Now let's control the size of our text.

blocks.title: Font Size
blocks.output: The heading becomes larger than the paragraph.

blocks.text: The font-size property controls how large text appears.
The value 36px is a measurement.
The px unit represents CSS pixels.
You will learn more units later, but pixels are useful for understanding the fundamentals.

blocks.question: Which declaration changes the text color of an element?
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. The color property controls text color.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Think about the CSS property specifically designed for foreground text color.
blocks.reasoning: color changes the foreground color, while background changes the element's background.

blocks.text: Spacing and the Box Idea
A professional interface is not only about colors.
Spacing is one of the things that makes an interface easier to read and use.
CSS gives us two fundamental spacing properties called padding and margin.
Padding creates space between an element's content and its inside edge.
Margin creates space outside the element.

blocks.title: Padding and Margin
blocks.output: The card receives internal padding and external margin.

blocks.text: Pause here and picture the difference.
Padding gives the content breathing room inside the card.
Margin separates the card from other elements around it.
This distinction becomes extremely important when you start building layouts.

blocks.title: Different Padding Values
blocks.output: The first value controls vertical padding and the second controls horizontal padding.

blocks.text: CSS can accept different numbers of spacing values to control different sides.
You will explore the complete box model in a later lesson.
For now, remember the most important distinction: padding is inside and margin is outside.

blocks.question: A card's text is touching the card's edges. Which property should you increase?
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. Padding creates space between the content and the inside edge.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Think about whether the missing space is inside or outside the card.
blocks.reasoning: If the content is too close to the element's edge, padding creates internal space.

blocks.text: Borders and Rounded Corners
Our card has spacing now, but we can make its boundaries clearer.
The border property allows us to create a visible boundary around an element.

blocks.title: Adding a Border
blocks.output: The card receives a thin light border.

blocks.text: The border declaration contains a width, a style and a color.
Here the width is 1px.
The border style is solid.
The final value is the border color.
Modern interfaces also commonly use rounded corners.

blocks.title: Rounded Corners
blocks.output: The corners of the card become rounded.

blocks.text: The border-radius property controls the roundness of an element's corners.
A larger value generally produces more rounded corners.
Small details like spacing, borders and corner radius can make a simple component feel much more polished.

blocks.question: Which property is used to create rounded corners?
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Look for the CSS property that combines border with radius.
blocks.reasoning: border-radius controls the radius of an element's corners.

blocks.text: Connecting CSS to HTML
So far we have written CSS, but now we need to understand how CSS files are connected to HTML.
There are three common ways to apply CSS.
They are inline CSS, internal CSS and external CSS.
Inline CSS is written directly inside an HTML element.

blocks.title: Inline CSS
blocks.output: The h1 receives a blue text color directly from its style attribute.

blocks.text: Internal CSS is written inside a style element in the HTML document.

blocks.title: Internal CSS
blocks.output: The style element contains CSS inside the HTML document.

blocks.text: External CSS is written in a separate stylesheet file.
External CSS is especially useful for larger websites and applications.

blocks.title: Connecting style.css
blocks.output: The HTML document connects to the external stylesheet style.css.

blocks.text: The link element tells the browser to load the stylesheet.
The href attribute tells the browser where the stylesheet is located.
This separation allows your HTML and CSS to remain easier to organize as your project grows.

blocks.question: Which code correctly connects an external CSS file called style.css?
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. The link element connects an external stylesheet.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Look for the HTML element specifically designed to link a stylesheet.
blocks.reasoning: The link element with rel="stylesheet" and the correct href connects the external CSS file.

blocks.text: Notice how several CSS properties work together to create one visual component.
The background creates the card surface.
The padding creates breathing room inside the card.
The border defines the card boundary.
The border-radius rounds the corners.
The max-width prevents the card from becoming unnecessarily wide.
The margin declaration helps center the card horizontally.

blocks.question: Which property prevents the card from growing beyond the specified width?
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. max-width sets an upper limit for the element's width.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Look for the property that defines the maximum allowed width.
blocks.reasoning: max-width prevents an element from becoming wider than the specified maximum.

blocks.text: Finish the Interface
The structure is ready, so now let's finish the visual design.
Start with the main title.

blocks.title: Styling the Title

blocks.text: Now style the description.

blocks.title: Styling the Description
blocks.output: The description becomes readable with comfortable line spacing.

blocks.text: The line-height property controls the vertical space between lines of text.
Readable line spacing becomes increasingly important when your application contains larger amounts of text.
Now let's create the primary button.

blocks.text: Run the page again.
Look at the difference between the original HTML and the styled version.
The HTML structure did not need to become complicated.
CSS transformed the presentation of that structure.
This is the foundation of the interfaces you will build later in this course.
Think Like a CSS Developer
Before we finish, I want you to change your mindset about CSS.
Do not think of CSS as a collection of random properties that you memorize.
Think of CSS as a system for describing the visual relationships between elements.
When something looks wrong, first identify which element is responsible.
Then identify the selector that targets that element.
Next, identify the property that controls the part you want to change.
Finally, choose an appropriate value.
That simple process will help you solve many CSS problems.
If a button needs a different color, find the button selector and change its color property.
If text is too close to the edge of a card, think about padding.
If two components are too close to each other, think about margin.
If the corners need to be rounded, think about border-radius.
If the text is difficult to read, think about font size, color, line height and spacing.
You are no longer simply copying CSS.
You are beginning to understand how CSS decisions create an interface.

blocks.question: A paragraph is too close to the inside edge of its card. What is the most direct solution?
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. Padding creates internal space between the content and the card's edge.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Focus on where the unwanted closeness occurs: inside the card.
blocks.reasoning: Padding controls the space between an element's content and its inner boundary.

blocks.question: You want five buttons to share exactly the same styling. Which approach is most appropriate?
options: Give each button a different ID and write five separate rules.
Give each button the same reusable class and style that class.
Use inline CSS on every button.
Create five different element selectors with the same declarations.
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. Reusable classes are ideal for shared component styling.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Think about which selector is specifically designed to be reused across multiple elements.
blocks.reasoning: Classes are reusable and allow many elements to share one consistent styling rule.

blocks.question: Which statement best explains the relationship between HTML and CSS?
options: HTML controls appearance while CSS defines the document structure.
HTML provides structure while CSS controls visual presentation.
HTML and CSS perform exactly the same job.
CSS provides structure while HTML only controls colors.
blocks.correctFeedback: Excellent. Understanding this separation is fundamental to web development.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Return to the core idea of this lesson: structure versus presentation.
blocks.reasoning: HTML defines the document's content and structure, while CSS controls how that content is visually presented.

blocks.text: Lesson Complete
You have completed your first CSS lesson.
You now know what CSS is and why it is important.
You know the difference between selectors, properties and values.
You have used element selectors, class selectors and ID selectors.
You have changed colors, text sizes, backgrounds, spacing, borders and rounded corners.
You also connected an external stylesheet to an HTML document.
Most importantly, you built a small interface instead of only reading definitions.
In the next lesson, we will go much deeper into CSS selectors.
You will learn how to target elements more precisely and combine selectors to control larger interfaces.
Keep experimenting with the code you wrote today.
Change the colors, change the spacing, change the sizes and observe what happens.
The fastest way to become comfortable with CSS is to write a rule, run it and observe the result.
